paras: The killing of William Brown took place in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, early on July 31, 1910, when Police Officer Herman Weins shot dead Brown, a Black packing-house worker accused of shooting two officers hours before. During the search, a crowd of about a thousand men demanded that he be lynched, and part of it stoned a house occupied by Black residents. The story ran as far as Kentucky and Ohio, and two South Dakota editors wrote that the state had narrowly escaped a lynching.

Brown had come to Sioux Falls about two months earlier, worked at the packing plant, boarded at Sam Wortham's place nearby, and claimed army service. According to J. A. Fowler, a white witness, the trouble began in Henry Levinger's saloon when a young man walked close on Brown's heels "in a joking way," and Brown called them "all manner of ugly names." Fowler said Brown later drew a revolver on them near the Cataract hotel, where he was with six other Black men, and that Fowler then reported him to Officer James Collins.

On Saturday night, July 30, Collins tried to arrest Brown on Phillips avenue; in Fowler's account Collins partly threw him to the ground, and Brown broke loose and fired, hitting Collins below the heart. Brown escaped into an alley, and the wire account said he fired at several young women as he fled.

Searchers armed with shotguns, rifles and pistols combed the vacant All Saints school grounds, threatening to hang him. Part of the crowd surged to the county jail and looked through it despite Sheriff Nelson's assurance that Brown was not there. Later a crowd made threats and threw stones at a house on Eleventh street occupied by "colored people" until officers induced it to disperse. The wire credited officers and "cooler heads among the mob" with preventing an attack on Black homes.

Martin Ellingson, a former Deadwood police chief sworn in as a special officer, met Brown near the Queen Bee mill, fired without effect, and was shot in the leg. About 1 a.m., Weins, watching near Wortham's house, turned his flashlight on a figure and, by the officers' account, faced a revolver that "snapped but missed fire" before he shot the man through the forehead.

The local account said the crowd went home quietly once Brown was reported dead, while the Webster Reporter and Farmer wrote that it dispersed only after seeing his body. No report of an inquest or of arrests for the stoning appears in the coverage. By late September Collins was nearly ready to return to duty, but a surgeon said Ellingson's right foot would have to be amputated.

The fullest account, a Sioux Falls text reprinted by the Turner County Herald and other South Dakota weeklies, called Brown "the crazed negro" and a "desperate character," wrote that searchers hoped for "a crack at the coon," and said the demonstration against "the peaceable colored population" had no "serious intent."

A Sioux Falls special telegram in the Omaha Daily Bee on August 1, headed "Man Hunt in Sioux Falls; Negro Killed," became a wire story that Dakota weeklies ran as "Rioting at Sioux Falls" or "Race Riot in Sioux Falls." Shortened as "Negro Killed by Officers," it reached Kentucky and Ohio, while a Marshalltown, Iowa, paper headlined its report "Policeman's Bullet Cheats Mob of Its Prey."

Two South Dakota editorials drew different lessons: the Reporter and Farmer wrote that northern whites, like southern ones, sought vengeance on a Black man "without the formality of a trial" and was thankful the officer's shot had spared the state "a lynching bee." The Turner County Herald blamed the saloons, said it was "the white man who first provoked the negro," and objected to the "further pestering of the blacks by the whites." All accounts came from officers and white witnesses; no Black newspaper account has been found.

Reports place Ellingson's wound six inches above the knee, above the left knee, in the knee, or, in the surgeon's later account, in the right thigh. A short Nebraska wire said Brown fired at Weins and missed, rather than misfired, and placed the killing in the south side residence district.

reader.title: Killing of William Brown
bases: A Sioux Falls policeman, Herman Weins, shot Brown dead during a manhunt after Brown was accused of shooting two officers, while a crowd of about a thousand searched and demanded a lynching (A2, A7, A1).

A local Sioux Falls account (A2, A7), a separate special telegram (A1), a separate short wire (A4) and a later DeSmet summary (A21) agree that Weins killed Brown after Collins and Ellingson were shot, though all rest on officers' and white witnesses' versions.

accounts.label: J. A. Fowler (white witness)
accounts.gist: A friend of Fowler's jokingly walked on Brown's heels in Levinger's saloon; Brown cursed them, later drew a revolver near the Cataract hotel, and when Collins seized him and partly threw him down, broke loose and fired three times.

accounts.label: Local Sioux Falls account (officers' version)
accounts.gist: Weins, watching Wortham's house, turned his flashlight on Brown, whose revolver snapped and missed fire, and killed him with one shot; the paper said Brown meant to 'get' as many policemen as possible.

accounts.label: Sioux Falls special telegram / wire
accounts.gist: Brown fired at several young women as he fled; about 1,000 men searched, many demanding a lynching, and pleading by officers and 'cooler heads among the mob' prevented an attack on Black homes.

accounts.label: Short wire (Beatrice, Norfolk)
accounts.gist: Brown 'called on colored friends' after the insult; a 'posse of a thousand' searched, and Weins found him in the south side residence district, where Brown fired and missed before Weins killed him.

accounts.label: Hurley editor
accounts.gist: The trouble was due to the saloons, the white man provoked Brown first, and the affair was being used to further harass Black residents.

framing.detail: The local Sioux Falls account called Brown 'the crazed negro' and 'a desperate character' and quoted searchers hoping for 'a crack at the coon', while saying the demonstration against Black residents had no 'serious intent'.
The wire story, headed 'Man Hunt in Sioux Falls', 'Rioting at Sioux Falls', 'Race Riot in Sioux Falls' or 'Negro Killed by Officers', gave the officers' version and praised the 'well directed shot'.

The Reporter and Farmer said the mob's demand for Brown's life showed northern whites sought vengeance 'without the formality of a trial', and was thankful the officer's shot saved the state from a lynching.
The Turner County Herald editorial blamed the saloons and the white man who 'first provoked the negro', and objected to the 'further pestering of the blacks by the whites'.
The Marshalltown headline 'Policeman's Bullet Cheats Mob of Its Prey' framed the killing as forestalling a lynching.
